[MUQATIL:101:7-8/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Only sincere monotheists make their scales heavy by saying there is no god but God; they enjoy a pleasing life in Paradise and never become dissatisfied there.
[TAB:101:7/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī explains the contented life as a life in Paradise that the person is pleased with.
[TAB:101:7/r2] TAB, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda glosses the contented life as being in Paradise; the source gives no grading.
[TAB-FULL:v24p594#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the person is in a life he is pleased with in Paradise. | mentions 69:21
[TAB-FULL:v24p594#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada glosses the pleasing life as Paradise. | mentions 69:21
[ZAJJAJ:v5p355/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Some gloss rāḍiyah as “pleasing,” which returns to the same exegetical meaning: a life that satisfies its inhabitant.
[NAHHAS:v5p280/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The Arabic construction means ‘a life possessing satisfaction,’ a relational adjective.
[NAHHAS:v5p280/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · مجاهد | reports | He says the person will be pleased with the life.
[SULAMI:v2p416/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | In answer to whether deeds make scales heavy, the Wāsiṭī says God makes them heavy or light as He wills; a report says the scales are in God's hand, who raises and lowers people according to pre-eternal decree.
[MAWARDI:101:7/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | Qatada takes the phrase as a pleasing life, namely Paradise.
[MAWARDI:101:7/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak understands it as lasting bliss, construing it from ʿaysh (life) rather than maʿash (livelihood).
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p328/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says the approved life is a pleasing life, namely Paradise.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p328/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak says it is lasting bliss.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p444/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | Another account says a substance will be created for each component of a person's acts, and those substances will be weighed as the deeds' measure.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p444/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Those whose scales are heavy with good deeds will have a pleasing life; “pleasing” means made pleasing to them.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p444/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | reports | One account says deeds are weighed through the weighing of their written records.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p264/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq explains a pleasing life as one of satisfaction that its possessor likes, using possessive adjective patterns.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p264/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو بكر | reports | Abu Bakr explains such forms as meaning 'possessing milk, merit, and dates'; commentators therefore gloss the life as pleasing to its owner.
[WAHIDI-QT:101:7/r1] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | A pleasing life is a life that its inhabitant is pleased with.
[JISHUMI:v10p7519/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Rāḍiya has a passive sense, “pleasing,” or means “possessing satisfaction,” like other active forms used for what someone has.
[JISHUMI:v10p7519/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Two poetic examples support using an active form to mean “possessing” something, as in “possessing hardship” or “possessing dates.”
[BAGHAWI:101:7/r1] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | The person is in a pleasing, approved life in Paradise.
[BAGHAWI:101:7/r2] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj explains the phrase as a life possessing satisfaction, one its owner is pleased with.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p511#2/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The person with heavy scales lives in a pleasing life in Paradise.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p511#2/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj explains radiya as possessing contentment: the person is pleased with that life.
[IBNATIYYA:101:7/r1] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh explain rāḍiya as a life endowed with satisfaction, an attributive construction expressing relation.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p516#3/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalil and Sibawayh explain radiyah as a possessive adjective: a life possessing satisfaction.
[TABRISI:101:5-11/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A pleasing life is one its owner is content with.
[RAZI:101:7/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | ʿĪsha is a verbal noun meaning living or life, just as khīfa means fear.
[RAZI:101:7/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj explains rāḍiya as a life possessing satisfaction, one its owner approves, like labin and tāmir meaning possessing milk and dates; commentators gloss it as pleasing to its owner.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | ʿĪsha is a verbal noun meaning living, just as khīfa is a verbal noun meaning fear.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj interprets rāḍiya as a life possessing satisfaction that its owner approves; the exegetes paraphrase it as pleasing to its owner.
[QURTUBI:101:7/r1] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | One meaning is a pleasing life that its owner is satisfied with.
[QURTUBI:101:7/r2] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another reading makes the life itself the giver of satisfaction: it is gentle and compliant with its inhabitants.
[QURTUBI:101:7/r3] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Paradise’s raised couches, about a hundred years high, lower for a friend of God to sit on and then rise again.
[QURTUBI:101:7/r4] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | A tree’s high branches bend its fruit within reach when the friend of God desires it, whether sitting or standing. | mentions 69:23
[QURTUBI:101:7/r5] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Wherever the friend of God walks or moves, a river runs with him in whatever direction he wants, above or below. | mentions 76:6
[QURTUBI:101:7/r6] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | reports | A report says he points with his staff and a river flows without a channel wherever he wants among his palaces and halls.
[QURTUBI:101:7/r7] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | These blessings make the life itself seem to grant satisfaction, yielding freely and generously to its inhabitants.
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A pleased life can mean a life that is pleasing to its owner.
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Alternatively the life itself actively gives satisfaction by its softness and submission to its occupants; Paradise's raised couches lower for a saint and rise afterward.
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Paradise's fruit branches lower toward a saint when desired, illustrating the Qur'anic description of near fruit. | mentions 69:23
[QURTUBI-FULL:101:7-9/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A report says a saint's staff makes a river flow without a channel through his palaces and gathering places wherever he wishes. | mentions 76:6
[BAYDAWI:101:7/r1] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | The life is endowed with satisfaction.
[BAYDAWI:101:7/r2] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Alternatively, the life is pleasing to its inhabitant.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:101:1-11/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The person enjoys a life that is itself pleasing or is pleasing to its inhabitant.
[NASAFI:101:7/r1] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The life is either endowed with pleasure or itself pleasing and approved.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p354#7/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | A life pleasing in itself may mean one filled with satisfaction or one that is made pleasing to its inhabitant.
[QASHANI:101:1-5/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | This annihilation reading does not fit the later distinction of heavy and light scales; in God’s scale, rising and ascending count as weight, while descent is lightness: enduring righteous deeds matter most, and perishable pleasures have no weight.
[QASHANI:101:6-10/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Heavy scales are real sciences, psychic virtues, and heart and spirit perfections; their owner has a satisfied, true life in gardens of attributes above gardens of deeds.
[ABUHAYYAN:101:6/r2] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The segment also refers the expression “a pleasing life” to Abu Hayyan's discussion of it in al-Haqqa. | mentions 69:21
[ABUHAYYAN:101:7/r1] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Abu Hayyan again refers discussion of the scales and their heaviness and lightness to al-Aʿraf. | mentions 7:8, 7:9
[ABUHAYYAN:101:7/r2] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Abu Hayyan refers the expression “a pleasing life” to his discussion of it in al-Haqqa. | mentions 69:21
[IBNKATHIR:101:7/r1] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | A pleasing life means life in Paradise.
[BIQAI:101:7/r1] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The blessed life is a life in which its inhabitant continually moves and lives.
[BIQAI:101:7/r2] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The feminine form suggests a single, constant state of clarity and pleasure rather than the varied conditions of worldly life.
[BIQAI:101:7/r3] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The life either possesses satisfaction or is pleasing; its abode is the lofty Garden. | mentions 101:9
[BIQAI:101:9/r4] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Hāwiya is an extremely low, descending fire in which he keeps falling; the passage omits a hostile life in the second clause and a mother in the first. | mentions 101:7
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p514/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | A person whose good deeds outweigh falsehood enters a life of lasting, consistent pleasure; rāḍiya can mean either possessing satisfaction or being pleasing.
[DURR:101:6/r3] DURR, d. 911 · قتادة | reports | Qatada identifies the heavy-scale person's pleasing life as Paradise. | mentions 101:4, 101:5, 101:8, 101:9

[ALUSI:101:6/r1] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The passage summarizes the division of people into two groups and signals each group's particular state after describing what is common to all.
[ALUSI:101:7/r1] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The common analysis takes rāḍiya as a relational adjective: a life characterized by satisfaction or delight.
[ALUSI:101:7/r2] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Rāḍiya can mean pleasing, with the word figurative for the passive sense or attribution transferred from the person enjoying the life.
[ALUSI:101:7/r3] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | A further proposal analyzes the expression as a concealed metaphor with an associated imaginative image.
[ALUSI:101:7/r4] ALUSI, d. 1270 · السيرافي | reports | Al-Sirafi objects that relational adjectives are not normally feminine because they do not agree with an overt described noun, yet rāḍiya carries feminine hāʾ.
[ALUSI:101:7/r5] ALUSI, d. 1270 · السيرافي | reports | Al-Sirafi offers two explanations: the life is pleased with its inhabitants and stays with them, or hāʾ marks intensity like ʿallāma and rāwiya.
[ALUSI:101:7/r6] ALUSI, d. 1270 · السيرافي | reports | Al-Sirafi also suggests that the suffix preserves the form by preventing loss of yāʾ, and notes feminine hāʾ in forms such as nāqa mashliya and kalba mujriya.
[ALUSI:101:7/r7] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Alusi's first answer is that rāḍiya is not relational here: it is an active participle meaning what follows necessarily from choosing and being pleased, or a figurative attribution.
[ALUSI:101:7/r8] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | His second answer is that hāʾ can indicate intensity and is not restricted to the faʿʿāla pattern, as rāwiya shows.
[ALUSI:101:7/r9] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | His third answer allows hāʾ to preserve the form in a defective word and exceptionally in miṣakka, with a doubled form analogized to a weak one.
[ALUSI:101:9/r8] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الكشف | reports | Al-Kashf calls the imprecation reading best because it matches the emphatic wording of the preceding pleasurable life; al-Tibi calls it clearest, though al-Alusi leaves room for discussion. | mentions 101:7
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The well-known interpretation takes rāḍiya as a relational adjective: the life is one endowed with contentment or satisfaction.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | He accepts intensive h as an explanation, noting that this suffix is not confined to the pattern faʿʿāl, as riwāya also shows.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | He also accepts adding h to a weak adjective to preserve its form; misakka is either an irregular form or reflects geminates’ resemblance to weak roots.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | He also allows rāḍiya as a figurative passive meaning pleasing or pleased-with, or a figurative attribution whose true subject is the life’s possessor.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A concealed metaphor with an imaginative metaphorical feature is another possible analysis, as discussed in works of rhetoric.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض الاجلة | reports | A distinguished scholar argues that relational adjectives mean ‘possessing such-and-such’ and therefore are not feminine, since they do not modify an expressed noun and are treated as nouns.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السيرافي | reports | Al-Sīrāfī objects that the feminine h in ʿīsha rāḍiya challenges the claim that relational forms do not take feminine marking.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السيرافي | reports | One explanation makes the life pleased with its inhabitants, accompanying them and content with them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السيرافي | reports | A second explanation treats the feminine h as an intensive suffix, as in ʿallāma and riwāya.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السيرافي | reports | The h may preserve the word’s form by preventing loss of yāʾ; similar weak adjectives and some forms otherwise not feminized show this usage.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p222/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Alusi explains rāḍiya here as an active participle whose necessary implication is intended: whoever wants and accepts something necessarily stays with it; the attribution may also be figurative.
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Calling the life rādiyah rather than marḍiyyah is rhetorically emphatic: the life so fully satisfies its worthy owner that it surrounds him with lasting contentment. | mentions 89:27, 89:28, 89:29, 89:30
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Âlûsî | reports | Alusi says the familiar reading takes rādiyah as a relational form, meaning a life characterized by satisfaction.
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Rādiyah may also be understood as marḍiyyah by lexical or predicative metaphor, meaning a life its owner is pleased with.
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Rhetoricians also allow a concealed and imaginative metaphor in the expression.
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · بعض الإجلة | reports | Some eminent scholars object that relational forms are construed with dhū and are not made feminine because they attach to nouns rather than functioning as adjectives.
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Sîrâfî | reports | Sirafi gives three explanations for the feminine ending: the life stays attached to its people, the ending intensifies meaning as in rāwiya, or it preserves the word's form after loss of yā.
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Sîrâfî | reports | Sirafi says the intensive feminine ending is not limited to allāma and cites rāwiya as another example; misakka may be anomalous or analogical.
[ELMALILI:101:6-7#2/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Âlûsî | prefers | Alusi praises Sirafi's analysis as a subtle explanation missing from most books.
[QUTB-ZILAL:101:7/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Quṭb leaves the pleasant life undescribed in detail so its shade of contentment is felt; this is the most restful bliss.
[IBNASHUR:101:7/r1] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur says عيشة is a verbal noun from العيش, like خيفة from الخوف, and here means life.
[IBNASHUR:101:7/r2] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Calling the life راضية is a rational metaphor: its possessor is content with it, so the life is described that way because it causes contentment or is its time.
[TABATABAI:101:1-9/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Meccan surah warns and gives glad tidings about resurrection, with warning as its dominant tone.
[TABATABAI:101:1-9/r12] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | In 'a satisfying life,' 'life' with kasra is a noun of kind like sitting; calling the life satisfied is figurative attribution, or means a life possessing satisfaction.
[TABATABAI:101:10-11/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · القمي | reports | Al-Qummi glosses those whose scales are light as people with little good. | mentions 101:6, 101:7
[ASAD-NOTES:101:intro/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | This is an early Meccan surah, probably revealed after At-Tin (surah 95). | mentions 95:1
[CORPUSCORANICUM:101:7:anmerkung/r1] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | The wording parallels 69:21 and 88:9; other early Meccan uses of r-d-y occur at 93:5, 92:21, 89:28, and 53:26, giving the root an apparently consistent eschatological association. | mentions 69:21, 88:9, 93:5, 92:21, 89:28, 53:26
[CORPUSCORANICUM:111:3-5:kommentar/r5] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | Riddling that creates rhetorical tension also structures oath sequences such as Q 100 and teaching questions at 90:12–16, 97:2–4, 101:1–11, and 104:5–9. | mentions 100:1, 90:12, 90:13, 90:14, 90:15, 90:16, 97:2, 97:3, 97:4, 101:1, 101:2, 101:3, 101:4, 101:5, 101:6, 101:7, 101:8, 101:9, 101:10, 101:11, 104:5, 104:6, 104:7, 104:8, 104:9
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p421/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Only deeds will help: God weighs them in a just balance, granting eternal bliss when good deeds outweigh evil and Hell when the scales tip the other way.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p424/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Only deeds matter on that Day; good deeds that outweigh evil bring salvation, while the rest doom their bearers, and a special balance weighs human deeds. | mentions 21:47
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:101:6/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | prefers | Mawazin may mean the things weighed, namely deeds; the translation prefers this reading.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:101:6/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | reports | Alternatively, mawazin is the plural of mizan, “scales,” but metonymically still means the deeds weighed.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:101:6/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Heavy deeds signify an abundance of good that earns God's approval and eternal happiness in richly provisioned Gardens.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:101:6/r5] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Since afterlife events are unseen beyond what revelation states, one cannot speculate about how deeds will actually be weighed or measured.
[STUDYQURAN:101:6/r8] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The contenting life of the person with heavy scales is linked to 69:21. | mentions 69:21
[STUDYQURAN:101:intro/r3] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The final six verses contrast the recompense of those whose scales are heavy with good deeds and those whose scales are light.
